analysis.title: PCE: Real After-Tax Income Fell in September, With Real Spending Flat; Inflation Picked Up
key_insights: Nominal personal income rose 0.2% in September, the weakest growth since April. Wages and salaries rose 0.3%. Disposable income also rose 0.2%.

Nominal consumer spending rose 0.5% in September, more than after-tax income, so the personal saving rate fell to 3.8% from 4.0% in August. This is the lowest since late 2022 and, outside that period, the lowest since the Great Recession.
PCE price index rose 0.5% m/m in September, the highest since March when the U.S. conflict with Iran started. Gasoline and other energy goods prices jumped more than 9% on the month.
Core PCE rose 0.3% m/m in September, the same as August and up from 0.1% in June and July.

On a year-ago basis, headline PCE inflation was 3.6% in September, up from 3.4% in July and August. Core PCE was 3.1% y/y, the first time at that level since May. Both have been above the Fed's 2% target since 2021.

Real after-tax income fell 0.3% m/m in September, the first decline since April. Real disposable income growth was 1.0% y/y (0.95% before rounding), the first sub-1% reading outside April since late 2022.
Real consumer spending was flat in September. Real durable goods spending fell 0.8%, nondurables were flat, and real services rose 0.2%. Real spending was up 2.5% y/y, down from 2.7% in August.

PNC says the data support a 25 basis point fed funds hike at the FOMC meeting on December 8-9, and expects a further hike at the mid-March meeting, taking the range to 4.25%-4.50% by early spring. Fed funds futures price an 83% probability of a December hike.
PNC cites the strong stock market and a falling saving rate as supports for spending, with no guarantee they hold. The July 2026 saving rate was revised up to 4.5% from 3.0% in the prior release.

tension_points.bear_case: Real after-tax income fell 0.3% m/m, the saving rate is at 3.8%, and the softer labor market and high inflation are stretching consumers.
